stories.title: Boris and Igor - The Inequality Parable
stories.description: Two Russian farmers: Boris has a goat, Igor doesn't. Igor complains to the authority that it's unfair. The authority asks what he wants. Igor says 'Kill Boris's goat.' Now they're equal - both have no goat. This Stephen Pinker story captures the moral confusion between inequality and poverty.
stories.learning: Equality can be achieved by making everyone equally poor. But what matters is poverty reduction. When growth happens, some get richer faster, increasing inequality, but everyone can be better off in absolute terms. India's choice since 1991 shows this: poverty fell, inequality rose, millions came out of destitution.

stories.title: The Psychology of Privilege and Virtue Signaling
stories.description: Amit observes wealthy people in air-conditioned rooms discussing socialism, degrowth, and other fashionable beliefs that harm the poor they claim to care about. They feel virtuous without living with consequences of their policy preferences.
stories.learning: Privilege allows divorced morality from outcomes. A wealthy person can afford to be anti-growth and pro-socialist because they've already escaped poverty. The poor don't have that luxury. Intention doesn't matter - impact does.

stories.title: Child Labor Paradox - Oxfam and UNICEF Studies
stories.description: When Western activists pressured factories over child labor, 30,000-40,000 children were laid off in Bangladesh and Nepal. Many girls went into prostitution. Many boys turned to crime. Their lives became worse, not better.
stories.learning: Good intentions without understanding incentives and choices cause harm. Parents don't want children working - they do it because it's their best option. Without growth creating better options, banning child labor just moves children to worse alternatives. This is a luxury belief - easy for elites to hold, devastating for those affected.

recommendations.title: Defending the Undefendable
recommendations.author: Walter Block
recommendations.why: Amit's key recommendation for this episode. Block takes seemingly indefensible positions (like defending sweatshops and prostitution) and shows the logic. He's teaching people to think rigorously beyond tribal dogma. If you're uncomfortable with his arguments, that's a sign you need to engage more carefully with your own thinking.

recommendations.title: On Inequality
recommendations.author: Harry Frankfurt
recommendations.why: Frankfurt's doctrine of sufficiency: what matters is everyone reaching an adequate level of living, not equality. This intellectual move reframes the entire debate. Instead of fighting over who has more, focus on lifting everyone above subsistence. Frankfurt is the philosopher version of what Amit argues as economist.

recommendations.title: Vision of the Anointed
recommendations.author: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.why: Directly quoted in this episode. Sowell shows how visions of the anointed (those who believe they're on a higher moral plane) make policy based on feeling virtuous rather than on evidence. The title's subtitle is 'Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy.' Essential for anyone wanting to identify their own biases.

recommendations.title: In Defense of Globalization
recommendations.author: Jagdish Bhagwati
recommendations.why: Amit mentions Bhagwati's work on how free markets and globalization have lifted billions out of poverty. Counter to fashionable anti-capitalist sentiment, backed by evidence. Essential for anyone who wants the actual economic history.

core_ideas.explanation: Rob Henderson's concept: ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while inflicting costs on the lower classes. Socialism, degrowth, price controls, victimless crime bans - these are affordable beliefs for those who've already escaped poverty. The poor bear the actual costs.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: Makes visible the hidden structure of much elite discourse. Many intelligent, well-meaning people unknowingly advocate policies that harm the vulnerable while making themselves feel virtuous. Understanding this isn't cynical - it's empathetic to those who actually live with consequences.

core_ideas.idea: Inequality vs. Poverty - They're Different Problems
core_ideas.explanation: Inequality is the gap between rich and poor. Poverty is absolute deprivation. You can have high inequality with everyone better off (US has more inequality than Bangladesh, but Americans are richer). Conversely, you can reduce inequality by making everyone equally poor. The policy tools are different: inequality needs redistribution, poverty needs growth.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: India's moral imperative is poverty reduction. With hundreds of millions still in destitution, the focus on inequality is a luxury belief. Growth inevitably increases inequality but reduces poverty. The tradeoff is real - choosing equality over growth just makes everyone poorer.

core_ideas.idea: The Power of Compounding in Growth Rates
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay illustrates: 2% per capita growth vs. 4% growth. At 2%, doubling takes 35 years. At 4%, it takes 16 years. Over 32 years (visible planning horizon), the 4% growth path means 4x income vs. 2x. A small difference compounds into a massive divergence. This is why growth-destroying policies are so harmful.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: Luxury-belief policymakers don't see the massive human cost of lower growth. What feels like moral stands (degrowth, price controls, socialism) translate into millions of people stuck in poverty for additional decades.

core_ideas.explanation: Sweatshops are terrible working conditions that people choose over alternatives like farming or prostitution. They represent the best available option, not oppression (barring actual coercion/trafficking). Making sweatshops illegal doesn't eliminate bad conditions - it eliminates the least-bad option, pushing workers into worse situations.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: Respecting human agency means recognizing people as making rational choices within constraints, not as victims needing saving. Growth that creates better options is the answer, not bans that eliminate current options.

core_ideas.idea: Victimless Crime Prohibition and Unintended Consequences
core_ideas.explanation: Banning prostitution, betting, alcohol: all move these activities underground where the underworld takes over. Without rule of law, coercion becomes rampant. The Matunga racket: cops would pose as clients, then extort gay men. Price controls create black markets. Bans don't stop activity - they stop regulation and protection.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: The desire to legislate morality (left or right) crashes into reality: you can't ban human behavior. You can only choose between legal/regulated or illegal/exploitative versions.

core_ideas.idea: Preference Falsification and Social Media Tribalism
core_ideas.explanation: Timur Kuran's concept: people say what gains them advantage or status, not what they believe. On social media, once you stake a position, tribe membership and ego keep you locked in. The algorithm amplifies extremism because moderates lose status.
core_ideas.why_it_matters: We can't assume people really believe luxury beliefs - they may just be status-seeking. And that status-seeking gets locked in by social media dynamics. Understanding this prevents bitter judgment and opens space for actual conversation.

jokes_and_cultural_references.moment: Amit cannot resist the pun: 'Luxury beliefs' (Louis Vuitton reference) about luxury beliefs (expensive-to-poor opinions)
jokes_and_cultural_references.cultural_significance: Meta-humor on the concept itself - the name is clever wordplay. Sets tone for deconstructing trendy ideas through language.

jokes_and_cultural_references.moment: The Bruce Yandle essay 'Baptists and Bootleggers' - those calling for bans work with beneficiaries of prohibition
jokes_and_cultural_references.cultural_significance: A framework for understanding 'moral' coalitions that align rich moralists with bootleggers. The evangelist and the bootlegger both want alcohol banned for different reasons.

jokes_and_cultural_references.moment: Amit's criticism of the film 'Raees' where Shah Rukh Khan plays a bootlegger opposing a politician calling for alcohol ban
jokes_and_cultural_references.cultural_significance: Pop culture meets economics. In reality, they'd be aligned - both want prohibition. The movie missed the actual political economy.

jokes_and_cultural_references.moment: Amit on social media: 'I know one song from 2017 and one from 2018, the rest is from 1992'
jokes_and_cultural_references.cultural_significance: Self-deprecating observation about aging out of cultural relevance, transitions naturally into discussion of staying open to new ideas.
